text: In the days of Elijah's faith, ravens fed him. In the day of his depression, the Lord Himself fed him.
explanation:
When Elijah was full of faith, God sent ravens with bread and meat, then a widow whose flour and oil never ran out. But after he fled from Jezebel and lay under a broom tree asking to die, the Angel of the Lord Himself touched him, baked him a cake on the coals and gave him water. Then He let him sleep and did it all again.

You might think God keeps His distance when you're discouraged, doubtful or burned out. It's the opposite. In your lowest moment, He comes closer, and He serves you Himself.

text: "The journey is too great for you." God knows. That's why He feeds you first.
explanation:
The second time the angel woke Elijah, he said, "Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you." There's no rebuke in those words, just understanding. God knew exactly how far Elijah had to go and how little he had left.

You may be looking at the road ahead (the bills, the deadlines, the diagnosis, the responsibilities) and thinking it's more than you can carry. God agrees. That's why He gives you bread from heaven. Elijah "went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights." Keep coming and keep feeding on His Word.

text: Elijah's only recorded personal prayer was "Take my life." God refused, and Elijah never died at all.
explanation:
Under the broom tree, Elijah prayed, "It is enough! Now, Lord, take my life." God didn't answer that prayer. Instead, unknown to Elijah, a chariot of fire was waiting to carry him to heaven without ever tasting death.

Sometimes God's "no" is the kindest answer He gives. He wasn't going to let His tired servant die discouraged in some lonely desert. He had something far better planned. When He doesn't answer the way you asked, He's preparing to do "exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think."

text: "What are you doing here, Elijah?" For God to ask that, He had to be there too.
explanation:
God never asked "What are you doing here?" at the brook, at Zarephath or on Mount Carmel, because He had sent Elijah to each of those places. But Horeb was Elijah's own idea, a retreat to the mountain of the law, fleeing a woman's threat.

Yet notice: God was there waiting for him. Even when you've walked into a valley of your own making, He will never leave you nor forsake you. He'll ask you gently what you're doing there, and then lead you out.

text: When Elijah saw Jezebel's threat, he ran. The man who'd said "the Lord before whom I stand" now lived by sight.
explanation:
Elijah had once told a king, "As the Lord God of Israel lives, before whom I stand." He was conscious of the invisible God. But when Jezebel's message came, "he saw" and ran for his life. He forgot the ravens, the widow's flour, the boy raised from the dead and the fire from heaven, all because one angry face loomed larger than the living Lord.

Peter was walking on water until he saw the wind. The enemy always works through the visible: the report, the bill, the person who intimidates you. Moses "endured as seeing Him who is invisible." Keep your eyes on Him.

text: Just because the brook dried up doesn't mean God didn't send you there.
explanation:
God sent Elijah to the brook Cherith and fed him there for a season. Then "after a while the brook dried up." It wasn't a sign Elijah had missed God or done something wrong. God simply had a new place for him, and a widow in Zarephath who needed to be blessed.

When a job, a season or a ministry dries up, don't assume it was never God's will. (This doesn't apply to your marriage!) Ask Him, "Where is my 'there' now?" Provision waits where He sends you, and so do people He wants to bless through you.

text: Scripture says God is rich in mercy and grace. It never says He's rich in wrath. Isaiah calls judgment His "strange work."
explanation:
God is a righteous judge, and sometimes He must act in judgment. But look for a verse that calls Him "rich in wrath" and you won't find one. You will find "rich in mercy," "abounding in grace," "plenteous in mercy." Isaiah calls His act of judgment "His unusual act," "His strange work." Micah says, "He delights in mercy."

Even Elijah's famine lasted three and a half years, half of seven. Like a parent who must discipline a child, God's hand may act, but His heart is always full of love. And He chose for the fire of judgment to fall on His Son instead of on you.
